title: Wolverines versus the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, and Bix's debt to New Orleans
summary: Hug relays Cy Gerard's comparison and argues Bix worshipped New Orleans musicians.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: What, as close as you can figure out, what was the style of that Wolverines group? Was it, did they connect it all with any more?
The Wolverines, as I once spoke to a fellow around here that used to play saxophone. I don't know if you ever did get to meet him, Cy Gerard.
Never did. You told me about him, I never met him.
Wonderful character. It's too bad that you missed him.
Yeah, we wanted to get together.

He was the most, he was a very, very, very charming, interesting person. He was one of these fellows, I never did know too much about his saxophone player, but he knew everything. You could ask him something about what was happening, you know, and one of these kind of fellows, he could tell you everything that was happening and always knew everything. And he knew everything about the New Orleans Rhythm Kings and everything that happened. And once I was talking to him and he told me something that I had in my mind and he told me the same thing and it coincided exactly what I had in mind. He says, don't you think, Oman, he says that the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, or rather, how did he put that now? The New Orleans Rhythm Kings was an improvement on the original Dixieland Jazz Band.
And he says, don't you think that the Wolverines was an improvement on the New Orleans Rhythm Kings? Of course, that's kind of putting it kind of strong.

And I am from New Orleans, and I hate to say this, but I do think that in some respects that maybe the Rhythm Kings was some kind of an improvement in many ways. As far as harmonies and new ideas, you know, for little introductions and endings and things that the Rhythm Kings were playing very simple things. They were playing things that was real, basic New Orleans music, which is nothing wrong, which I dearly love. But, of course, we must admit that Bix came along and did change things to a degree, because, after all, his solos were so inventive.
And right now I realize that I'm getting into talking about Bix, which you haven't really asked me too much about yet.

Well, we're getting up to it, and I think one of the things that we're getting to is how the New Orleans musicians influenced him. And what we owe to the New Orleans musicians, or New Orleans for, you know, there's a big controversy about this.
And some say he departed very radically from it.

Well, I think that this is a very good thing to think about. That's why I have no misgivings about saying that the Wolverines was an improvement on the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. But I'm only meaning that from, you know, constructive criticism, because I do think that Bix basically worshipped New Orleans musicians deep in his heart, even though he was far advanced in his theory. He basically...
